tweets: Pilgrims have climbed this hill for over a thousand years believing it's a giant stone serpent frozen mid-coil — and today, tens of thousands do it again every single day.

The hill is called Seshachalam, "mountain of Shesha" — the cosmic serpent Vishnu reclines on in scripture. Its seven peaks are said to be Shesha's seven hoods, so pilgrims call it Saptagiri, the Seven Hills.

The Venkateswara temple atop it isn't a medieval add-on. Tamil poet-saints called Alvars were already singing hymns to "Venkatadri" by the 6th-9th centuries CE, long before most of Europe's great cathedrals existed.

Vijayanagara emperor Krishnadevaraya poured wealth into the shrine in the early 1500s. Bronze statues of him and his two queens still stand at the temple entrance, hands folded, exactly where he placed them 500 years ago.

A hill named for a serpent's hoods now sees more footsteps in a single day than most monuments see in a month. Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
